\chapter{The Colour German Lent Away}
\label{ch:schwarz-weiss}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say black and white in German, and name the German word Romance borrowed for white.}

German's colour words are home-grown, with no Latin borrowed in -- and one of them emigrated. schwarz is Germanic swartaz, which English kept only in the dusty corner of swarthy; weiss is hwitaz, which English kept whole as white. Then blank, a German word for shining, went the other way: it became the word for WHITE in French, Italian and Portuguese, pushing Latin albus out of everyday use. After nineteen chapters of German buying words from Rome, this is the chapter where Rome's daughters buy from German.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[schwarz]{schwarz — \textquotedblleft{}black\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-schwarz}



\begin{quote}
Four colours are coming, and not one of them was borrowed. That is rarer than it sounds.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: schwarz}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{schwarz} — \textquotedblleft{}black.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

One word, two consonant clusters, and no Latin in sight. German's colour vocabulary is \textbf{home-grown}: where the months came in wholesale from Latin, the colours stayed Germanic.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{schw-cluster} — \emph{sch} is English \emph{sh}, and the \emph{w} after it is a \emph{v}. So the word opens \emph{shv-}, which English never does at the start of a word. Take it slowly: \emph{sh} … \emph{v} … and then run them together.
  \item \texttt{z-ts} — a German \emph{z} is always \emph{ts}, never English \emph{z}. The word ends \emph{-arts}.
\end{itemize}

Put together: \emph{SHVARTS}.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the opening cluster alone — \textquotedblleft{}shv, shv\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}schwarz\textquotedblright{} — \emph{SHVARTS}
  \item the two clusters apart, then together — \textquotedblleft{}shv … arts … schwarz\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, schwarz.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}black.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Schwarz}.) How does the word open? (\emph{\textbf{Shv-}} — \emph{sch} plus a \emph{w} that is a \emph{v}.) How is a German \emph{z} sounded? (\textbf{Ts}.) Was it borrowed from Latin? (\textbf{No} — the colours are inherited.) Next: the English cousin it left behind.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[schwarz und swarthy]{schwarz, taken apart}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-schwarz-swarthy}



\begin{quote}
English has this word too. It has been reduced to one dusty corner of the dictionary.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Schwarz} comes from Germanic *\emph{swartaz}. English inherited the same word — and then \emph{black} took over the everyday job, leaving the old one alive in exactly one place:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{swarthy} — \textquotedblleft{}dark-complexioned\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That is \emph{schwarz}, worn down and pushed to the edge. Say the pair aloud and the family shows: \emph{schwarz} · \emph{swarthy}.

Further back there is a Latin relative, and it is not flattering. The root behind *\emph{swartaz} also gave Latin \emph{sordēs}, \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{dirt}\textquotedblright{} — which English took as \textbf{sordid}. Black and grubby turn out to be one idea seen twice: the colour of soot, and the state of being covered in it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, swarthy\textquotedblright{}
  \item the Latin relative — \textquotedblleft{}sordēs, sordid\textquotedblright{}
  \item the idea they share — \textquotedblleft{}the colour, and being covered in it\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, swarthy.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \emph{schwarz}'s cousin? (\emph{\textbf{Swarthy}}.) What does it mean? (\textbf{Dark-complexioned}.) Which English word comes from the Latin relative? (\emph{\textbf{Sordid}}, from \emph{sordēs} \textquotedblleft{}dirt\textquotedblright{}.) Next: the second colour, and the letter that only German has.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[weiß]{weiß — \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-weiss}



\begin{quote}
Black's opposite, and the first ordinary word in this book that needs the letter you were shown back in the writing chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: weiß}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{weiß} — \textquotedblleft{}white.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Three letters and every one of them is a trap for an English eye. It is pronounced, near enough, like English \textbf{vice}.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{w-is-v} — German \emph{w} is English \emph{v}. The word opens \emph{v-}.
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ei} — German \emph{ei} is the vowel of English \emph{eye}. Never \textquotedblleft{}ee\textquotedblright{}.
  \item \texttt{ss-eszett-long} — and here is the \textbf{ß}, doing exactly what you were told it does: marking a sharp \emph{s} after a \textbf{long} vowel. You met that in the writing chapter with nothing to spend it on. \emph{Ei} is long, so the \emph{s} is written \textbf{ß} and sounded sharp. This is the word that spends it.
\end{itemize}

So \emph{weiß} rhymes with \textbf{vice} — not with the second half of \emph{vice versa}, where the \emph{s} is soft.

You already know what Switzerland does with that letter, and \emph{weiß} is the word where you will see it: Swiss German writes \textbf{weiss}, with the ß spelled out.
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}weiß\textquotedblright{} — like English \emph{vice}
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß\textquotedblright{}
  \item the rule out loud — \textquotedblleft{}long vowel, sharp s, written ß\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}white.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Weiß}.) Which English word does it rhyme with? (\emph{\textbf{Vice}}.) Why is the \emph{s} written \textbf{ß}? (\textbf{The vowel before it is long}.) How does Switzerland write it? (\emph{\textbf{Weiss}}.) Next: the English word it is, under the spelling.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[weiß und white]{weiß, taken apart}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-weiss-white}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Schwarz} needed a fossil to show its English cousin. This one needs nothing.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Weiß} comes from Germanic *\emph{hwītaz}, and so does English \textbf{white}. Not a cousin, not a borrowing — the \textbf{same word}, and neither language moved its meaning by a hair.

What separates them is spelling and nothing else:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{German} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
the vowel & \emph{ei} & \emph{i} \\
the sharp \emph{s} & \textbf{ß} & \emph{t} plus a silent \emph{e} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That is the whole distance. \emph{Weiß} and \emph{white} look unrelated on the page and are identical underneath, which is a useful warning about judging these pairs by eye: \textbf{schwarz}/\emph{swarthy} looked close and had drifted in meaning, while \emph{weiß}/\emph{white} looks distant and has not drifted at all.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}weiß, white\textquotedblright{}
  \item the ancestor — \textquotedblleft{}hwītaz\textquotedblright{}
  \item both colours and both cousins — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz swarthy, weiß white\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}weiß, white — one word.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which English word is \emph{weiß}? (\emph{\textbf{White}} — the same word.) Did its meaning drift? (\textbf{No}.) Which of this chapter's two pairs drifted in meaning? (\emph{\textbf{Schwarz}}/\emph{swarthy}.) Next: a German colour word the Romance languages took.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[blank]{blank — \textquotedblleft{}shiny\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-blank}



\begin{quote}
A word that looks English, is German, and means neither of the things you would guess.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: blank}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{blank} — \textquotedblleft{}shiny,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}polished,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}bare.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Not \textquotedblleft{}blank\textquotedblright{} in the English sense of empty-of-writing, and \textbf{not} a colour. A polished shoe is \emph{blank}; a bare sword is \emph{blank}. The idea underneath is \textbf{shining}.

Hold on to that meaning exactly as it is, because the next lesson is about what happened when the neighbours borrowed it and let it drift.

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{vowel-a} — short and clipped, the \emph{a} of English \emph{hat}.
  \item \texttt{ng-cluster} — the \emph{-nk} closes with the back-of-the-mouth \emph{n} that English puts in \emph{bank}, and then a real \emph{k}.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}blank\textquotedblright{} — shiny, not empty
  \item what it is not — \textquotedblleft{}not a colour\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three colours so far and the odd one out — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß … blank\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}blank — shiny.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{blank} mean in German? (\textbf{Shiny, polished, bare}.) Is it a colour? (\textbf{No}.) Does it mean English \textquotedblleft{}blank\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{No}.) Next: what the Romance languages did with it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[blank, blanc, bianco]{The word that emigrated}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-blank-blanc}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Blank} means shining. In three languages next door, it means \textbf{white}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
In its Frankish form \emph{blank}, \textquotedblleft{}shining,\textquotedblright{} this word was \textbf{borrowed into Romance}. Once there it stopped meaning shiny and started meaning white — and it displaced Latin's own word for white, \emph{albus}, almost entirely:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{language} & \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{}} \\
\midrule
French & \textbf{blanc} \\
Italian & \textbf{bianco} \\
Portuguese & \textbf{branco} \\
German & \emph{blank} — still only \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{shiny}\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Latin's \emph{albus} survives in English only in learned scraps: \emph{albino}, \emph{album} (originally a white tablet), \emph{albumen}. The everyday Romance word for the commonest colour there is came \textbf{from Germanic}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
This runs \textbf{against the usual current}. Almost everywhere else in this book the lending goes the other way: Latin hands words to Germanic, and German takes them. \emph{Wein} came from Latin \emph{vīnum}; the month names came over wholesale and are still Latin under a German spelling.

Here, once, Germanic did the lending — and the two sides then went different ways with it. German kept the original sense and never made it a colour; the borrowers made it a colour and let the shine fall away.

A word does not carry its meaning with it when it crosses a border. It carries only its sound, and the new language decides the rest.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three borrowers — \textquotedblleft{}blanc, bianco, branco\textquotedblright{}
  \item the German original — \textquotedblleft{}blank, and it still means shiny\textquotedblright{}
  \item the direction — \textquotedblleft{}Germanic lent this one; usually Latin lends\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}blank, blanc — one word, two meanings.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which three Romance words came from \emph{blank}? (\textbf{Blanc, bianco, branco}.) Which Latin word did they push out? (\emph{\textbf{Albus}}.) Does German \emph{blank} mean white? (\textbf{No} — still shiny.) Which way does the lending usually run? (\textbf{Latin to Germanic} — as with \emph{Wein} and the month names.) Next: the two colours together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — black, white, and the one that left}

\label{lesson:GE-C13-schwarz-weiss}



\begin{quote}
No new words. Two colours, three words, and two families that behaved in opposite ways.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{German} & \textbf{where it came from} & \textbf{what English or Romance did with it} \\
\midrule
\emph{schwarz} & Germanic *\emph{swartaz} & English kept it only in \emph{swarthy} \\
\emph{weiß} & Germanic *\emph{hwītaz} & English kept it whole, as \emph{white} \\
\emph{blank} & Frankish \emph{blank} & Romance took it and made it \emph{white} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Three words, three fates: one nearly lost, one perfectly preserved, one emigrated and changed job.

You cannot put these into a sentence yet — German needs a verb for that and it is still several chapters away. Bank the words; the sentence comes later.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the two colours — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß\textquotedblright{}
  \item them with their English cousins — \textquotedblleft{}schwarz swarthy, weiß white\textquotedblright{}
  \item the emigrant and its children — \textquotedblleft{}blank; blanc, bianco, branco\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three fates — \textquotedblleft{}kept, lost, emigrated\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}schwarz, weiß, blank.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say both colours. (\textbf{Schwarz, weiß}.) Which one is the same word as its English cousin? (\emph{\textbf{Weiß}}/\emph{white}.) Which survives in English only as \emph{swarthy}? (\emph{\textbf{Schwarz}}.) Which German word became \textquotedblleft{}white\textquotedblright{} abroad? (\emph{\textbf{Blank}}.) Why is \emph{weiß} written with \textbf{ß}? (\textbf{Long vowel before a sharp s}.) Next: the other two colours, and a cousin that is not a borrowing.
\end{tcolorbox}
